title: Left hemicolectomy and sigmoid colectomy
subtitle: Ureter first, the right tie, a tension-free colorectal join

Guidelines for perioperative care in elective colorectal surgery: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) Society recommendations: 2018 (Gustafsson UO et al., World J Surg)

indications: Adenocarcinoma of the sigmoid or descending colon (sigmoid colectomy or left hemicolectomy with oncological lymphadenectomy), as recommended by the MDT.
Splenic flexure cancer: left hemicolectomy (or extended resection) including the left branch of the middle colic vessels, as the MDT plans.

Diverticular disease: elective resection for complicated disease (stricture, fistula to bladder or vagina) or for recurrent or persistent symptoms after a shared decision; not routinely after a single uncomplicated episode.
Sigmoid volvulus after decompression, where the patient is fit; endoscopically unresectable polyps.
contraindications: Generalised faecal or purulent peritonitis with a physiologically unstable patient: a Hartmann's procedure or damage control is the safer operation (see Hartmann's procedure).
Acute uncomplicated diverticulitis, which is treated without surgery.
A frail patient in whom the risks of resection outweigh the symptoms of benign disease.
Laparoscopy specifically: inability to tolerate pneumoperitoneum or a fixed phlegmonous mass beyond the team's experience.
preparation: Colonoscopy (or CT colonography) to define the lesion and exclude synchronous cancer; tattoo small lesions. In diverticular disease, exclude cancer within a stricture.
Cancer: CT chest, abdomen and pelvis, CEA and MDT decision. Fistula: CT or cystoscopy to define the tract.
Mark a left iliac fossa colostomy site and a right iliac fossa ileostomy site.
ERAS preparation, anaemia correction, nutritional screening; bowel preparation per unit policy.
Consider ureteric stents for a large inflammatory mass or a re-operative pelvis, as the unit prefers.

Consent: anastomotic leak, bleeding, ureteric, bladder, splenic and small bowel injury, conversion to open, defunctioning or end stoma, ileus, wound and port-site hernia, VTE, and a change in bowel habit.
positioning: Modified Lloyd-Davies with legs in padded stirrups, thighs flat, arms tucked, for transanal stapler access.
Head down and right side down for the pelvic and medial dissection; head up and right side down for the splenic flexure.
Secure the patient against sliding before tilting; check the common peroneal nerve at the stirrup.
equipment: Laparoscopic stack, 30-degree scope, atraumatic graspers, energy device, clips or vascular stapler.
Linear stapler for distal transection; circular stapler and anvil; sizers.
Wound protector; air leak test materials.
Open set immediately available; ureteric stents if planned.
anatomy: The descending and sigmoid colon are supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery (left colic and sigmoid branches) and the marginal artery; the splenic flexure has a variable supply from the left branch of the middle colic artery.
The inferior mesenteric vein runs separately, lateral to the duodenojejunal flexure, to join the splenic vein behind the pancreas.
The left ureter and gonadal vessels lie in the retroperitoneum beneath Toldt's fascia; the ureter crosses the iliac bifurcation at the pelvic brim.
The rectosigmoid junction is where the taeniae coli splay out to form a continuous longitudinal muscle coat, near the sacral promontory.
criticalSafety: Identify the left ureter before dividing the vascular pedicle or the mesentery.
For diverticular disease, make the distal anastomosis on the upper rectum (below the splay of the taeniae), not on residual sigmoid: an anastomosis on the sigmoid is associated with recurrence.
For cancer, take the mesentery with the lymph nodes to the level the MDT plans and handle the tumour as little as possible.
Before the anastomosis: perfused, tension-free, untwisted, doughnuts complete, air leak test negative.
structuresAtRisk: Spleen and tail of pancreas during flexure mobilisation
Bladder and vagina in diverticular fistula
Marginal artery and middle colic vessels
commonErrors: Dissecting too deep and lifting the ureter with the mesocolon.
Anastomosing onto sigmoid colon in diverticular disease.
Insufficient mobilisation, leaving a tense anastomosis.
Tearing the splenic capsule by pulling the flexure down.
In an inflammatory mass, trying to find planes from the inflamed side instead of starting in normal tissue and working towards the mass.
complications: Ureteric injury (may present late as urinoma or fistula).
Ileus, small bowel obstruction, wound infection, port-site hernia and VTE.
postop: ERAS pathway: early diet, mobilisation, opioid-sparing analgesia, early catheter removal.
Daily leak surveillance: tachycardia, fever, pain out of proportion, ileus, rising CRP; low threshold for CT.
Flank pain, a rising creatinine or watery drain output suggests a ureteric injury: test drain fluid creatinine and image.
Cancer: extended thromboprophylaxis per NICE and MDT review of the histology. Fistula: remove the urinary catheter only after the bladder repair has had time to heal per urology advice.

steps.emphasis: Both stoma sites marked. For benign disease, record that the decision to operate was shared and why.
State the indication (cancer or benign), because it changes the level of the vascular tie and the distal margin.
Modified Lloyd-Davies, arms tucked, secured for steep tilts in two directions.
Prepare the perineum as well as the abdomen; urinary catheter in.
For cancer, inspect the liver and peritoneum. For diverticular disease, define the extent of the inflamed segment and any fistula before dissecting.
In an inflammatory mass, start medially in uninflamed tissue at the promontory and find the ureter there, then work towards the mass.
Cancer: oncological tie of the inferior mesenteric artery; for a splenic flexure cancer, also divide the left branch of the middle colic vessels. Benign: divide close to the bowel.
Selective for a sigmoid colectomy; mobilise whenever the colon will not reach the rectum without tension.
Wound protector at the extraction site. Exteriorise the colon and choose the proximal division point.
Proximal division on soft, pliable, well-perfused colon. In diverticular disease it is not necessary to remove every diverticulum-bearing segment, only the thickened, diseased colon.

Sigmoid colectomy: colorectal end-to-end or side-to-end circular stapled anastomosis. For a splenic flexure left hemicolectomy with a colocolic join, a stapled side-to-side or handsewn anastomosis is used instead.
Air leak test for every colorectal anastomosis: saline in the pelvis, clamp above, air via the anus.
In emergency or contaminated surgery, a Hartmann's procedure or an anastomosis with defunctioning are valid outcomes, not failures.
Cancer: mark the high tie for the apical node. Fistula: send the bladder or vaginal margin separately if excised.
Close the extraction site fascia and every 10 mm or larger port.
Record ureter seen, level of tie, where the anastomosis lies (rectum or colon), doughnuts and air test, and the stoma decision.

step.lhc.distal-transection.title: Choosing and dividing the distal resection line
step.lhc.distal-transection.why: Where the distal line falls decides whether the operation cures the problem. In diverticular disease, residual sigmoid at the anastomosis is associated with recurrence; in cancer, the margin and the mesentery must clear the tumour.
how: Mobilise into the upper mesorectum just far enough to reach a soft, untethered segment; avoid unnecessary pelvic dissection in benign disease.
Diverticular disease: divide at the upper rectum, identified where the taeniae coli splay out into a continuous muscle coat.
Cancer: confirm the tumour position (tattoo, palpation or on-table endoscopy) and divide with the margin planned by the MDT, taking the mesentery at right angles to the bowel.
Divide the mesorectum or mesentery at the chosen level, then transect with a linear stapler in a single firing where possible, keeping the ureters and the vagina clear.
structuresAtRisk: Left and right ureters at the pelvic brim
pitfalls: Dividing at the level of the sigmoid in diverticular disease because the pelvis looked difficult.
Losing the tumour position in a laparoscopic resection because the lesion was not tattooed.
Multiple stapler firings that leave crossing staple lines.
